title: Red Lines for Developers and Techies
intro: Chapter 11: Red Lines for Developers and Techies

tips.title: Ask three questions before you act: whose interests might this harm, how likely is the other side to file a police complaint, and what evidence would exist? If a case is registered, engage a criminal lawyer that day.
tips.cost: No cost at all. Before acting, replace “Is this technically feasible?” with “Will the vendor, the platform or the company file an FIR?” The hard part is resisting the thought that nobody will bother about something this small. Server logs, UPI and bank statements, delivery addresses and chat backups are exactly what an Indian investigation asks for, and platforms preserve them on request.
tips.inPlainWords: Before doing anything, ask whether the company will go to the police. Logs, payment records and chats are easy to collect. In India a person who is arrested must be told the grounds of arrest, produced before a magistrate within 24 hours and allowed to consult a lawyer. If you cannot afford one, the State Legal Services Authority must provide one. The first 24 hours and the first bail hearing matter more than anything that happens later.
tips.benefit: Anyone who knows of an offence can complain. For a cognizable offence the police must register an FIR under section 173 of the BNSS, 2023; if they refuse, the complainant can go to the Superintendent of Police or to the magistrate. Arrest is not automatic, and bail is the rule rather than the exception. The Constitution guarantees the right to be informed of the grounds of arrest, to consult a lawyer of your choice (Article 22(1)) and to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours (Article 22(2)). Free legal aid is a constitutional promise under Article 39A, delivered through NALSA and the State Legal Services Authorities; call 15100. If the charge sheet is not filed within 60 or 90 days, depending on the offence, the accused becomes entitled to default bail.
tips.sources: Constitution of India. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Legal Services Authority. <https://nalsa.gov.in/>; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: There is no fixed countdown to an arrest decision as there is in some jurisdictions. What is fixed is the investigation clock: the charge sheet must come within 60 or 90 days, and bail is decided by a magistrate or court, not by the police. A lawyer is most useful before the first remand hearing, to check the grounds of arrest, oppose police custody and move for bail. Do not sign a statement in the police station; under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 a confession to a police officer is not admissible. Every other item in this chapter turns on the same question: whether the other side has grounds to complain and the money to pursue it.

tips.title: Refuse to build or sell game cheats, including “AI assistants” that only read the screen
tips.cost: There is no monetary cost. The trade-off is the income from cheat orders and “small tools”. The difficulty is that this money arrives quickly and it is never clear which game publisher will eventually complain.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no user-count or rupee threshold for this. Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000 punishes unauthorised access to a computer resource, or damage to it, with up to three years and a fine of up to five lakh rupees, and section 43 lets the owner sue for damages. A cheat that edits game memory, fakes a server response or lifts assets out of the client is the exposure. Separately, cracking the game's protection is an offence under section 65A of the Copyright Act, 1957, and selling copies is infringement under section 63.
tips.benefit: The IT Act does not require a minimum number of users or a minimum profit. What it requires is access without the owner's permission, or damage. Section 66 covers acts listed in section 43 done dishonestly or fraudulently, and section 43 covers unauthorised copying, downloading or extraction of data and disruption of a computer resource. A publisher can also sue for breach of its terms and for inducing players to breach theirs, and under the Copyright Act where a cheat copies or redistributes game code or art. If the tool steals player accounts it can attract section 66C (identity theft) and section 66D (cheating by personation) as well.
tips.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Office. <https://copyright.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: No reported Indian judgment decides whether a screen-reading assistant that never touches memory is an offence. The practical test is whether the tool talks to the game's servers or copies its code without authorisation; if it only watches the screen the IT Act case is weak, but the publisher can still enforce its terms and pursue copyright claims if assets are copied. Enforcement is driven by the publisher's complaint, not by the tool's author. “It is only a single-player game” does not help: the licence terms and the copyright in the assets apply either way.

tips.title: Do not write or sell scripts for ticket booking, flash sales, fake orders or coupon farming, even if they only “click a button faster”
tips.cost: No expense and no time required. Reading the platform's terms of use takes ten minutes and is the only real work.
tips.inPlainWords: A script that fires requests faster than a person is still automated access. IRCTC, the railway e-ticketing platform, and private ticketing and e-commerce sites prohibit it in their terms; using it can get the account and the payment instrument blocked and the bookings cancelled. Where the script gets past a login, a captcha or a rate limit, section 66 of the IT Act, 2000 applies, with up to three years' imprisonment and a fine. Selling the script to others adds abetment, and fake orders bring cheating.
tips.benefit: There is no Indian threshold of a fixed profit or loss figure. The exposure is built from four pieces: the platform's contract (account termination, blacklisting, damages), the IT Act, 2000 where access controls are bypassed (section 43 civil, section 66 criminal), the BNS, 2023 where money is taken by deception or an account is impersonated, and the Railways Act, 1989, which penalises unauthorised sale of tickets and touting. A flash-sale bot that holds inventory and resells it can also be proceeded against by the marketplace under its seller and buyer terms.
tips.sources: Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation. <https://www.irctc.co.in/>; Ministry of Railways. <https://indianrailways.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Consumer Affairs. <https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: Indian enforcement here is mostly platform-level: cancellations, blacklisting, frozen payouts and civil notices rather than reported criminal trials. That makes it easy to mistake for a technical game, which is the point of the tip. Do not build a “personal use” script and then share it; distribution is what turns a contract breach into a conspiracy or abetment case. A platform that suspects automation may also demand fresh KYC and hold the money while it investigates, which is a real cost even when no case is filed.

tips.title: Crawl only pages that need no login, never defeat an access control, never touch personal data, and never sell what you collect
tips.cost: No cost at all. A crawler is a program that fetches pages and extracts data. Before running one, read robots.txt and the site's API terms; robots.txt is the file in the site root that lists paths the owner does not want crawled. Anything behind a login, a token or a signature is out of scope. The real difficulty is self-discipline: the data is technically reachable, and that is exactly when the line gets crossed.
tips.inPlainWords: In India there is no fixed number of records that turns scraping into a crime. The questions are whether you were authorised, whether you got past a protective measure, and whether you took personal data. Bypassing a login or a block is unauthorised access under section 43 of the IT Act, 2000, and section 66 makes it criminal. Personal data brings the DPDP Act, 2023: notice, consent, purpose limitation, security. Selling the data makes every one of those worse.
tips.benefit: Public, unauthenticated pages are the part of the web a crawler may read. Once you defeat a rate limit, a captcha, an IP block or a login you are in section 43 territory: the site owner can claim damages, and section 66 can make it an offence punishable with up to three years and a fine. Under the DPDP Act, 2023 the person who decides why and how personal data is processed is a Data Fiduciary and owes notice, consent, purpose limitation, accuracy, security safeguards and breach reporting; the Schedule allows penalties running to hundreds of crores of rupees for security failures, failure to report a breach, and breaches concerning children. Compilations and databases are also protected as literary works under section 2(o) of the Copyright Act, 1957, so lifting a substantial part of a curated database can infringe copyright.
tips.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Office. <https://copyright.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Indian law has no general database right, and scraping facts that are truly public is not by itself unlawful; the liability comes from how you obtained the data and what you do with it. “Public” is not a permanent defence: a site can withdraw permission in its terms or with a technical measure, and continuing after that changes the analysis. If the crawl touches personal data, do not rely on “it was already public”; the DPDP Act still applies to the processing you do. Keep a record of the terms you relied on and the paths you crawled. If a dispute starts, that record is your defence.

tips.title: Refuse development orders for gambling, fraud or adult-content apps, and do not run payment rails or “account recovery” for those clients
tips.cost: No direct monetary cost. The trade-off is forgoing well-paid outsourcing work with vague requirements. The difficulty is that these clients usually pay above the market rate and are in no hurry to explain what the app does.
tips.inPlainWords: Building the app is not a neutral technical favour. India now bans online money games and their advertising, and state gambling laws cover betting that is not a game of skill. If the product takes money by deception you can be charged with cheating, and if you knowingly help, with abetment or criminal conspiracy. Taking a cut of the payments and unblocking accounts for a fraud ring is the version of this that ends in arrest.
tips.benefit: Four regimes apply. The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 prohibits online money games, and operating, playing, advertising or funding them carries criminal liability. State gambling statutes and the BNS, 2023 cover betting operations and cheating. The IT Act, 2000 covers unauthorised access (section 66), identity theft (section 66C) and cheating by personation (section 66D); adult content is covered by section 67 (obscene material), section 67A (sexually explicit material) and section 67B (child sexual abuse material), with the POCSO Act, 2012 for anything involving a child. On the payment side, the RBI's directions for payment aggregators and gateways require merchant due diligence and KYC, and a gateway that knowingly onboards a fraud merchant risks its authorisation and a money-laundering case under the PMLA, 2002.
tips.sources: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Reserve Bank of India. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: “I did not know” is judged on what a reasonable developer would have noticed: a fee far above the market, top-up and cash-out screens, betting logic, a client who will not say what the app is for, and a request to hide the app from store review. Those facts are used to prove knowledge. Indian investigators increasingly work backwards from the money, through UPI handles, mule accounts and payout wallets. Keep the written scope of work, the client's KYC and your invoices; if the client refuses to give them, that refusal is your answer.

tips.title: When you leave a job, hand back access and never delete data, leave a backdoor or change passwords
tips.cost: No cost. Ask for a written handover checklist and keep a copy.
tips.inPlainWords: Your employer owns the systems and the data. Deleting a database, leaving a backdoor, changing an admin password or copying client data can be an offence under the IT Act, 2000 and the BNS, 2023, and a breach of your contract. Return the laptop, the tokens and the credentials, and keep only your own employment records.
tips.benefit: The IT Act, 2000 punishes unauthorised access, data damage and identity misuse. The BNS, 2023 covers mischief and criminal breach of trust. The employer can sue for loss and obtain an injunction. A former employee who keeps a backdoor can be prosecuted even without a profit motive. A written handover protects both sides.
tips.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>
tips.caveats: Keep your own payslips and appointment letter; do not copy client data or source code. A non-disclosure agreement can survive resignation. If you find a security flaw, report it instead of testing it further.

tips.title: Do not take source code, client lists or technical documents when you leave; do not put them in personal cloud drives or reuse them at your next employer
tips.cost: No cost involved. Before you leave, delete every company file from your personal laptop and cloud drives, and hand back the devices and the accounts. The difficulty is that some files were written by you personally, which makes them hard to part with.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no trade-secrets statute. What protects the company is the contract you signed, the copyright in the code, and the access records on its systems. Code you wrote in the course of your job belongs to the employer under section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957; copying it out is infringement, and distributing it is a criminal offence. A client list is protected as confidential information under your NDA, and as a compilation under copyright in some cases.
tips.benefit: Section 17(c) of the Copyright Act, 1957 makes the employer the first owner of copyright in a work made in the course of employment under a contract of service, unless the contract says otherwise. Copying that code without authority infringes copyright under section 51, and section 55 gives the employer an injunction, damages, an account of profits and delivery up. Distributing infringing copies is an offence under section 63, punishable with imprisonment of six months to three years and a fine of fifty thousand to two lakh rupees. Under the IT Act, 2000, downloading data from an employer's system without authority falls under section 43, and section 66 makes the dishonest version criminal. Your confidentiality clause and any invention-assignment clause are enforceable as contracts, and a court can grant an injunction to stop you using the information long before the trial.
tips.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Office. <https://copyright.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: There is no Indian statute that defines a trade secret or sets a penalty for taking one, so any case is built from the contract and from copyright. Two things follow. First, a client list built from public sources is much harder to protect than one that carries pricing, contacts and notes. Second, the realistic remedies for a former employer are an injunction and damages; criminal charges under section 63 are usually brought against commercial piracy rather than one departing employee. If a new employer asks you to bring anything from the old job, get that request in writing and refuse it in writing. Appointment letters in India often carry a confidentiality and non-solicitation clause that survives resignation; read it before you accept the offer.

tips.title: Do not run your own programs on someone else's server or camera, and do not mine crypto on a company machine
tips.cost: No cost. Ask for written permission and a scope before any test. Do not install software on a machine you do not own.
tips.inPlainWords: Using a computer, server or camera you do not own without permission is unauthorised access under the IT Act, 2000. Installing a miner or a bot on a company machine can be data damage, theft of electricity and a breach of contract. Even a 'harmless' scan of a system you were not asked to test can be an offence.
tips.benefit: Section 66 of the IT Act, 2000 punishes unauthorised access and data damage, and section 43 allows civil damages. The BNS, 2023 covers mischief and theft of electricity. The employer can dismiss you and sue for the loss. A security researcher should work within a written scope and a safe-harbour policy.
tips.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: A public bug-bounty programme is a permission, but only within its scope. A 'read-only' scan can still be unauthorised access. Keep the permission in writing.

tips.title: Testing someone else's systems without written permission: “good intentions” and “reporting afterwards” are not a defence
tips.cost: No cost at all. Before you join a vendor's bug bounty programme or a public beta test, get a document that states the permitted scope, the target systems and the testing window. Once a vulnerability is confirmed, stop testing. The real challenge is resisting the urge to “give it a quick try”.
tips.inPlainWords: In India the question is not how many accounts you took or how much money you made. It is whether you had permission and how far you went into the system. Section 43 of the IT Act, 2000 lets the owner sue for unauthorised access, and section 66 makes it an offence where the access is dishonest or fraudulent, with up to three years and a fine. There is no safe harbour for research: good intentions do not create authority.
tips.benefit: Section 43 of the IT Act, 2000 covers access to, downloading from, copying from or extracting data out of a computer resource without the permission of the person in charge of it, and it gives the owner a claim for damages. Section 66 turns the same conduct into an offence when it is done dishonestly or fraudulently, punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or a fine up to five lakh rupees, or both. Section 66C covers identity theft and section 66D cheating by personation. If you were given credentials at work and used them outside the scope you were given, that is the clearest case against you: the authorisation was limited, and section 43 does not read it as permission to go further. Selling what you found can add criminal breach of trust under the BNS, 2023, and where personal data is involved, liability under the DPDP Act, 2023.
tips.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: India does not grade unauthorised access by counting credentials, machines or rupees, so the “nobody will notice one export” argument is weaker here, not stronger: there is no threshold to stay under. There is also no statutory safe harbour for security research. The only protection is a written authorisation that names the scope, the targets and the window; a bug bounty policy is such an authorisation only where it says so, and gratitude after the fact is not permission. Collect minimal evidence: a screenshot and a request identifier prove the finding without taking the data. If you have already gone further than you were authorised, stop, do not copy anything else, and take advice before you contact the vendor.

tips.title: Report a vulnerability privately and give the vendor time to patch; do not publish exploit code, and do not hand unreported findings to anyone who will use them
tips.cost: No cost involved. Report the vulnerability to the vendor or to CERT-In and hold the details until a patch exists.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no vulnerability-disclosure statute, so nothing here turns on a licence. What exists is a practice, coordinated disclosure, plus the IT Act, which makes access without authorisation an offence whether or not you meant well. Publishing working exploit code for a live system can make you a party to the access it enables. Personal data you copy out as proof brings the DPDP Act, 2023 with it.
tips.benefit: CERT-In is the national nodal agency for cyber incident response and is the body to notify when a vendor does not respond. The Directions issued under section 70B(6) of the IT Act, 2000 in April 2022 require service providers, intermediaries, data centres, body corporates and government organisations to report specified cyber incidents to CERT-In within six hours of noticing them, to keep logs for 180 days within Indian jurisdiction, and to synchronise their clocks to a network time source. Those duties fall on organisations, not on an independent researcher. The practice that Indian coordinators follow is the same one that keeps a researcher safe: tell the vendor first, give a reasonable time to fix, do not publish details of a live system, do not release a working exploit, and include the fix in anything you do publish.
tips.sources: CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Two warnings. There is no Indian rule that requires you to report a vulnerability, and none that bars you from reporting one to a foreign platform; the DPDP Act lets the government restrict transfers of personal data to specified countries, but that concerns personal data, not the fact of a bug. What does create exposure is how you got the finding: if you accessed the system without authorisation, that is section 43 and possibly section 66 of the IT Act regardless of what you do next. Keep the disclosure private, keep the evidence minimal, and keep a dated record of every message to the vendor; if the vendor is silent, escalate to CERT-In rather than to a public post. Do not name the customer whose data you saw, even in a private report.

tips.title: Do not sell network access you are not authorised to provide, and do not build a business on helping people get round a blocking order
tips.cost: No expense or time required. The step that matters is checking, before you take money, whether the service you are reselling is one you are authorised to provide.
tips.inPlainWords: India does not ban VPNs, and using one is not an offence. What is regulated is providing a telecommunication or internet service without authorisation, and what is risky is marketing a service whose whole purpose is to defeat a blocking order or to hide a customer's identity from a lawful investigation. Selling accounts or nodes you do not control also puts the customer's traffic in your hands, which brings the DPDP Act with it.
tips.benefit: The Telecommunications Act, 2023 requires authorisation to provide telecommunication services, and providing them without it is an offence under that Act; an internet service provider also needs a licence from the Department of Telecommunications. Reselling access you have no right to resell is a breach of the upstream provider's contract, and it ends with the accounts terminated and the customers' data exposed. Since the CERT-In Directions of April 2022, VPN service providers, cloud service providers and data centres must maintain subscriber, KYC and access records for five years and keep logs for 180 days. Where a blocking direction has been issued under section 69A of the IT Act, 2000, an intermediary that fails to comply with it is liable to punishment under that section; a product whose advertised purpose is to get round such an order invites the same attention, and a service that helps conceal a fraud or a data breach can be treated as part of it.
tips.sources: Department of Telecommunications. <https://dot.gov.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: India has no prohibition on private international gateways, no state monopoly on connectivity, and no penalty for a user who chooses a VPN; what remains regulated is providing a telecom or internet service without authorisation. So the Indian red line is narrower and it is commercial. Do not provide a telecom or internet service without authorisation, do not resell capacity you do not control, and do not advertise evasion of a lawful order. If you run a legitimate VPN or proxy product, the compliance work is subscriber KYC, five-year records, 180-day logs, a grievance officer and a clear statement of what you do with the traffic metadata.

tips.title: A non-compete that stops you working for a competitor after you leave is void in India; the clause that does bind you is confidentiality, so read that one
tips.cost: No cost involved. Find the offer letter and the appointment letter, keep the confidentiality and non-solicitation clauses to hand, and do not sign a fresh restraint at exit without reading it.
tips.inPlainWords: A non-compete clause says you may not work for a competitor for some period after you leave. In India, section 27 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 makes an agreement that restrains anyone from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business void to that extent, and the Supreme Court has applied that to post-employment restraints. There is no statutory compensation, no maximum term and no percentage formula, because the clause is simply unenforceable.
tips.benefit: Section 27 of the Contract Act, 1872 provides that every agreement by which anyone is restrained from exercising a lawful profession, trade or business of any kind is to that extent void; the only exception is a sale of the goodwill of a business. In Superintendence Company of India v. Krishan Murgai the Supreme Court held that a restraint operating after the termination of employment is void, not merely voidable. A restraint that operates during employment stands on different ground: an employee can be stopped from working for a competitor while still employed, and a notice period or garden leave clause is enforceable as a matter of contract. Confidentiality obligations and reasonable non-solicitation of clients are enforced through injunctions, because they protect information rather than restrain trade.
tips.sources: Indian Contract Act, 1872. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Labour and Employment. <https://labour.gov.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Three practical points. First, employers in India increasingly rely on the confidentiality clause and on the intellectual-property assignment in the appointment letter; a void non-compete does not free you to take documents or to use client and pricing data. Second, some letters are drafted as a non-solicitation or non-dealing clause precisely because a pure non-compete would fail; read the actual wording, not the heading. Third, the employer can still sue, and even a case it loses costs you time and can hold up a new job while an interim application is decided. If a former employer sends a notice, reply through a lawyer who does employment work, and do not discuss the new employer's systems with them.

tips.title: Code written in the course of your job belongs to your employer; keep personal projects on your own time and your own equipment, and never mix them
tips.cost: No cost involved. When you start a new job, read the intellectual-property and moonlighting clauses in your appointment letter. The main difficulty is that personal projects and work tasks often share one laptop, so the separation has to be deliberate.
tips.inPlainWords: Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957 gives the employer the copyright in a work made in the course of employment under a contract of service, unless the contract says otherwise. Software is a literary work, so code written for your job is the employer's. By contrast, India has no statutory rule that an employee's invention belongs to the employer: patent ownership follows the contract and the facts, and a hired-to-invent or assignment clause is what settles it. The author keeps the right to claim authorship and to restrain distortion, and that right cannot be assigned away.
tips.benefit: Two different rules apply to code and to inventions, and the appointment letter is where both are decided. Copyright: section 17(c) of the Copyright Act, 1957 makes the employer the first owner of a work created in the course of employment under a contract of service, and section 19 requires any assignment to be in writing and signed by the assignor. Patents: section 6 of the Patents Act, 1970 sets out who may apply for a patent, and only section 39 deals with inventions by employees of the government or a government undertaking; in private employment, ownership turns on the contract and on whether you were hired to invent, so an invention-assignment clause is what makes the employer the owner. Under section 57 of the Copyright Act the author keeps the right to claim authorship and to restrain or claim damages for distortion of the work.
tips.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Intellectual Property India. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>; Ministry of Corporate Affairs. <https://www.mca.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The trap is not the statute but the contract. Many Indian appointment letters assign all intellectual property created during employment, sometimes including work done outside office hours and on your own equipment, and some add a moonlighting clause that restricts outside work altogether. Read those clauses before you sign, and if a personal project matters to you, ask for a named exclusion in writing. Code written at home on your own laptop, with no company data, no company repository and no overlap with your duties, is the version that stays yours; a project that runs on company infrastructure or reads company data is not. Keep your personal repository on your own account and your own hardware, and never copy work code into it to “look something up”.

tips.title: If you build on GPL code, release your source under the same licence or replace the dependency; do not assume nobody will enforce it
tips.cost: No cost involved. Before you take a dependency, read its licence and run a licence scan over your dependency tree. The GPL family requires that a distributed derivative be licensed on the same terms and its source be made available, which conflicts with shipping a closed-source product. The hard part is giving up a library you have already built around.
tips.inPlainWords: An open-source licence is a permission with conditions, so using GPL code and refusing its conditions is copyright infringement, not a matter of etiquette. India has no separate open-source statute and no statutory multiplier for damages: the Copyright Act, 1957 gives the rights holder an injunction, damages or an account of profits, and a criminal complaint for commercial piracy. “The other side used GPL too” is not a defence.
tips.benefit: The Copyright Act, 1957 protects software as a literary work. Section 14 sets out the exclusive rights, section 51 defines infringement, and section 55 gives the owner an injunction, damages, an account of profits and delivery up. Section 63 makes infringement in the course of business a criminal offence carrying six months to three years and a fine of fifty thousand to two lakh rupees. A GPL licence grants permission only on conditions: distribute a derivative without releasing the source and you are outside the permission, so the distribution is unauthorised and the ordinary remedies apply. Section 65A, which protects technological measures, and section 57, which protects attribution and integrity, sit on top of that. A court can also order the infringing copies to be delivered up or destroyed.
tips.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Office. <https://copyright.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: India has produced very little reported litigation on open-source licences, so treat the risk as real but unquantified: no judgment sets a going rate for a GPL breach here, and there is no statutory multiple of damages. That is exactly why the practical answer is process rather than law. Keep a licence inventory, prefer permissive licences for closed products, and check the AGPL separately, because its network-use condition catches software you never ship as a binary. If a dependency is GPL and you cannot relicense, the cheapest fix is usually to replace it before launch, while the codebase is small. Do not rely on “we only use it on the server” unless the licence you are relying on actually says that.

tips.title: Collect only the personal data the app actually needs; get verifiable parental consent for anyone under 18, and write the notice in plain language
tips.cost: No cost involved. Before launch, compare the permissions the app requests with the notice you publish, and remove every permission that has no purpose behind it. The main difficulty is that product teams want to keep data “in case it is useful later”.
tips.inPlainWords: The DPDP Act, 2023 applies to personal data processed in India. It needs a lawful basis, usually consent, and consent has to be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action. Notice must be in plain language and available in English or any language in the Eighth Schedule. A child is anyone under 18: you need verifiable parental consent, and you may not track, behaviourally monitor or target advertising at children. Penalties are set in the Schedule and run to hundreds of crores of rupees, decided by the Data Protection Board.
tips.benefit: The obligations follow the data lifecycle. Section 4 requires a lawful basis for processing. Section 5 requires a notice stating what is collected, why, how to complain and how to withdraw consent. Section 6 requires consent to be free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous, given by a clear affirmative action, and limited to the purpose stated. Section 8 requires accuracy, reasonable security safeguards, and intimation of a personal data breach to the Board and to the affected person. Section 9 treats every person under 18 as a child, requires verifiable consent of a parent or lawful guardian, and bars tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children. Section 16 lets the Central Government restrict transfers of personal data to specified countries. The Schedule sets penalties, including up to two hundred and fifty crore rupees for a failure to take reasonable security safeguards, and the Data Protection Board of India decides them.
tips.sources: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>
tips.caveats: The word “necessary” is doing the work: collect what the feature needs, not what might be useful. In practice the choices sit with the product and engineering staff who pick the permissions and write the notice, even though the penalty falls on the organisation. Two common mistakes: treating a pre-ticked box or a bundled consent as consent, and treating a child as someone under 13 as some other laws do, which is not the test here. Keep a record of what you collect, where it is stored, how long you keep it and who you share it with; if the Board asks, that record is the answer. The IT Act, 2000 still applies alongside the DPDP Act, and section 43A requires a body corporate that handles sensitive personal data to compensate a person harmed by its failure to protect it.

tips.title: There is no website registration in India; what you must do is run an intermediary-compliant service, keep 180 days of logs, and report incidents within six hours
tips.cost: No registration fee, because there is no registration. What costs time is the compliance work: a published grievance mechanism, a retention policy for logs, and an incident procedure that someone can actually run at 3 a.m.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no ICP filing and no licence to launch a website or an app. Hosting is a commercial contract, not a permission from the state. What exists instead is a set of duties that begin once you have users: if you host other people's content you are an intermediary under the IT Rules, 2021 and need due diligence and a grievance officer; CERT-In requires 180 days of logs and reporting of specified incidents within six hours; and if you handle personal data the DPDP Act, 2023 applies. The nearest thing to a security classification is critical information infrastructure, which the government designates and which does not cover a small site.
tips.benefit: Three duties carry most of the weight. First, the IT Rules, 2021: an intermediary must publish terms of use and a privacy policy, appoint a grievance officer, acknowledge a complaint within twenty-four hours and resolve it within fifteen days, and observe the due-diligence duties in Rule 3(1)(b); a significant social media intermediary has additional duties under Rule 4, including a monthly compliance report and the identification of the first originator for certain offences. Second, CERT-In: the Directions of April 2022 require specified incidents to be reported within six hours of noticing them, logs to be kept for 180 days within Indian jurisdiction, and clocks to be synchronised to a network time source. Third, the DPDP Act, 2023, if you process personal data. Critical information infrastructure is designated under section 70A of the IT Act, 2000 and protected under the NCIIPC; designation is by government notification, not by self-assessment.
tips.sources: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre. <https://nciipc.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: India has no filing that a site must complete before it can host or resolve, and no classification assessment imposed on ordinary systems; do not pay for an ICP consultant and do not let a vendor sell you a classification audit you do not need. The 180-day log retention is real, and it is a floor rather than a target; longer retention brings the DPDP Act's storage limitation into play, so decide a retention period and write it down. Where the log contains personal data, the duty to keep it and the duty to minimise it have to be reconciled in the policy, not left to the engineer.

tips.title: Before you launch a generative AI service to the public, decide who is accountable for its output, label what it generates, and check the training data; India has no registration to do, which is not the same as having no duties
tips.cost: No registration fee, because there is no registration. The cost is the engineering: a labelling mechanism, a takedown route, an age gate where minors are involved, and a record of where the training data came from.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no pre-launch safety assessment and no algorithm registry. A public generative AI service is still subject to ordinary law: if you host user content you are likely an intermediary under the IT Rules, 2021, with due diligence, a grievance officer and a notice-and-takedown process; the DPDP Act, 2023 governs personal data in prompts and training sets; the Copyright Act, 1957 governs the material you trained on, and it has no text-and-data-mining exception. MeitY has issued advisories asking platforms to label synthetic content and to prevent deepfake harm, and those advisories are the closest thing to an AI-specific rule.
tips.benefit: Four duties, none of them exotic. Intermediary obligations: section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 gives safe harbour only to an intermediary that follows the due-diligence rules in the IT Rules, 2021, which means published terms, a grievance officer, action on a court order or a government direction, and removal of unlawful content within the timelines in Rule 3. Data: prompts and outputs are personal data when they identify someone, so the DPDP Act's notice, consent, purpose and security duties apply to them. Copyright: training on protected works and reproducing them in output are governed by the Copyright Act, 1957, and India has no exception for text and data mining, so a licence or another lawful basis matters. Blocking: section 69A of the IT Act allows a direction to block content, and an intermediary must comply.
tips.sources: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Office. <https://copyright.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The honest summary is that India regulates AI through existing law plus advisories, not through a registration regime. That makes the compliance work less bureaucratic and more substantive: you cannot point to a certificate, so you have to be able to explain your labelling, your takedown route and your training-data provenance. Two traps: assuming the service is not an intermediary because you generate the content rather than host it (the safe-harbour analysis turns on your role and your process, so take advice), and training on scraped personal data or copyrighted text on the theory that it is all public. If a model can produce a real person's likeness or voice, the deepfake advisories and the general law on personality rights apply, and minors' data requires verifiable parental consent under the DPDP Act.

tips.title: Do not build or distribute tools that strip ads out of someone else's app; charging nothing does not make it lawful in India, but ad-blocking is not a statutory offence either
tips.cost: No direct cost. The trade-off is giving up a popular utility. The psychological difficulty is that you took no money and only automated a tap the user would have made anyway.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no unfair-competition statute for this and no reported judgment holding an ad blocker liable. The exposure is elsewhere: modifying or injecting into another app's code, intercepting its network traffic, or copying its assets infringes copyright and can be unauthorised access under the IT Act, 2000. Distribution through an app store also binds you to the store's terms. Free does not make it lawful, and no Indian case gives you the “nothing happened” comfort a foreign precedent might.
tips.benefit: Four things can go wrong. Contract: the platform's terms of use and the app store's developer terms usually forbid interfering with another app or with its monetisation, and breach leads to removal and account termination. Copyright: modifying or redistributing another app's code or assets, or copying its ad-serving code, infringes under sections 14 and 51 of the Copyright Act, 1957, with remedies under section 55 and a criminal route under section 63. Access: if the tool intercepts or alters traffic, or attaches to another app's process, that is unauthorised access or damage under sections 43 and 66 of the IT Act, 2000. Data: an app that filters traffic sees the traffic, so if it sees personal data the DPDP Act, 2023 applies to what you collect and keep.
tips.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Competition Commission of India. <https://www.cci.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: India has no unfair-competition statute aimed at ad blocking: the Competition Act, 2002 addresses anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominance, and section 4 requires dominance and its abuse, which an ad blocker does not usually have. So the honest position is that a browser extension which filters the user's own browsing, on the user's own device, with the user's consent, has no clear Indian prohibition. What changes the answer is distribution plus interference: injecting into another app, stripping its branding, holding its traffic, or selling the resulting data. If you are building a legitimate ad or tracker blocker, publish what it does, keep it on-device, and do not touch another app's code.

tips.title: Do not resell model API access through an unlicensed proxy: you become the data controller for every prompt that passes through you, and you are probably in breach of the provider's terms
tips.cost: Zero financial outlay, and that is the trap: the margin looks like free money. The real cost is that you now hold other people's prompts, and the provider's terms give you no right to resell them.
tips.inPlainWords: India has no criminal offence for reselling API access and no licence for model aggregation. The risks are different ones. Reselling an account you bought as a company breaches the provider's terms and gets the key terminated. Routing other people's prompts through your server makes you a data fiduciary under the DPDP Act, 2023 and takes the data across borders. Using leaked or bulk-registered keys is unauthorised access under the IT Act, 2000. Selling a service that does not work is cheating under the BNS, 2023.
tips.benefit: Take the four in turn. Contract: model providers license access to a named entity on terms that prohibit resale, sharing credentials or building a competing product from the service; the remedy is termination, and reselling also breaches the confidence attached to the keys you were given. Data protection: under the DPDP Act, 2023 you determine the purpose and means of processing, so you owe notice, consent, security and breach intimation, and section 16 allows the government to restrict transfers of personal data to specified countries. Access: using keys that were not issued to you, or scraping tokens, is section 43 and possibly section 66 of the IT Act, 2000. Honesty: if you sell access you cannot supply, that is cheating under the BNS, 2023. Tax: reselling a service for a margin is a supply under the CGST Act, 2017, and once you cross the registration threshold you must register and charge GST.
tips.sources: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs. <https://cbic.gov.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>
tips.caveats: India has no reported prosecution of an API reseller for the reselling itself and no advisory aimed at relay operators, so do not plan around a criminal case; plan around the three civil consequences that do happen: the key is terminated, the customer sues for a service that stopped, and the data-protection duty attaches to you. If you want to build on models legitimately, the route is a business agreement with the provider, clear disclosure to users about where their data goes, a stated retention period, and a GST-compliant invoice. Anything that depends on an account you are not allowed to share is a business that ends the day the provider looks.

tips.title: Do not sell crack patches, keygens or cracked builds: circumventing a technical protection measure is itself an offence in India, and distributing pirated copies is a crime with no minimum value
tips.cost: Zero financial outlay. The cost is giving up the side income from cracked builds, registration keys and modified dongles. Never upload a crack to a public forum, a repository or a cloud drive. The psychological hurdle is that reverse engineering feels like craft rather than theft.
tips.inPlainWords: Licence checks, dongles and DRM are protected technical measures. Section 65A of the Copyright Act, 1957 makes it an offence to circumvent an effective technological measure for the purpose of infringing copyright, and section 63 makes distributing infringing copies a crime. India does not set a rupee threshold for either: the question is what you did and whether it was in the course of business, not how much you earned.
tips.benefit: Section 65A of the Copyright Act, 1957 punishes the knowing circumvention of an effective technological measure, where it is done to infringe a right conferred by the Act, with imprisonment up to two years and a fine. The same section preserves permitted purposes such as security testing, encryption research and interoperability, but it does not permit distributing a circumvention device or offering a service to others. Section 63 makes infringement in the course of business an offence carrying six months to three years and a fine of fifty thousand to two lakh rupees, and section 63A provides a longer term for a second conviction. Section 55 gives the rights holder an injunction, damages, an account of profits and delivery up, and section 65B covers the removal or alteration of rights-management information. Selling a key that does not work is also cheating under the BNS, 2023.
tips.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Copyright Office. <https://copyright.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The exemptions in section 65A are narrower than they look: they cover what you do for a permitted purpose, not the tool you hand to someone else. Private study and interoperability work can be defended; publishing the patch or selling the dongle cannot. India's criminal copyright provisions have no monetary trigger, so “I only made a little” saves you nothing on liability, though scale affects sentencing. Civil litigation is the likelier route, and it is slow and expensive: it ends in an injunction plus damages, and your costs are unrecoverable. If you maintain a patcher for legacy software, keep it to interoperability of your own data and get written permission before you share it.

tips.title: Never launch or help with a DDoS attack, never sell or rent a “stress testing” booter, and never flood a rival's server over a game dispute
tips.cost: Zero financial expense. A distributed denial-of-service attack overwhelms a target by pointing coordinated bot traffic at it. The cost is walking away from per-attack or subscription income, and keeping your temper in a game dispute or a business rivalry. Report the dispute to the platform or the police instead of buying an attack.
tips.inPlainWords: Knocking someone's site, server or game offline with a flood of traffic is unauthorised access and damage to a computer resource under the IT Act, 2000: section 43 gives the owner a civil claim, and section 66 makes it an offence with up to three years and a fine. Where the attack is meant to strike terror or to threaten the country's security or economic security, section 66F applies and carries the heaviest penalty in the Act. Paying someone to run the attack makes you a party to it.
tips.benefit: Section 43 of the IT Act, 2000 covers denial of access to a computer resource and disruption of it, and gives the person in charge a claim for damages. Section 66 makes the dishonest or fraudulent version an offence punishable with imprisonment up to three years, or a fine up to five lakh rupees, or both. Section 66F covers cyber terrorism, defined around acts intended to threaten the unity, integrity, sovereignty or security of India or to strike terror in people, and it carries imprisonment which may extend to life. Providing the tools is not a safe sideline: a person who supplies scripts, hosting or botnet access knowing what they are for can be charged as an abettor under the BNS, 2023, and selling a service that does not work is cheating. An attack on a rival business is also a civil wrong, and can be sued for damages.
tips.sources: Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; CERT-In. <https://www.cert-in.org.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: India does not have a separate DDoS offence, so cases are built from sections 43 and 66 and, where the facts are grave enough, section 66F. That matters in two ways: the sentence depends on the harm you caused rather than on a fixed threshold, and the first thing a target will do is preserve logs and file a complaint, which is why the traffic source is usually traceable. Stress testing is legitimate only on systems you own, or where you hold signed written authorisation that states the scope and the window. Booter customers are not anonymous: payments, chat logs and the booter's own records are what an investigation asks for.
